steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on detecting ChatGPT-generated academic writing. It should motivate the problem and why detection is hard, then walk through our dataset, the user study with human evaluators, the evaluation of existing detectors, and our own detector CheckGPT, followed by a contributions list, ethical considerations, and a paper roadmap.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation: ChatGPT text quality and misuse; need for detection tools
- Why LLM-content detection is hard; existing detectors and prior observations
- Dataset: GPABench2 (tasks, disciplines, prompts)
- User study and evaluation of existing detectors
- CheckGPT and its advantages
- Contributions
- Ethical considerations; paper organization

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
ChatGPT, the Large Language Model (LLM) that debuted recently, has shown it can generate sophisticated texts with a human-like language style and quality. People are concerned that LLM-generated content (LLM-content) can be misused to abuse the trust systems we have, for example in cheating and plagiarism, or in phishing and romance scams. Many academic institutes and publishers have announced policies about using LLM content, but these policies are hard to enforce unless there is a tool that detects LLM content accurately.

Detecting LLM-content can be challenging because of the unique characters of LLM/ChatGPT: (1) the output of an LLM is a relevant, organized response with few grammar errors, like a human conversationalist would give; (2) because of the sampling mechanism of LLM output, the choice of words is stochastic, so the responses are distinct even when the same inquiry is repeated multiple times; and (3) misuse of LLM-content can be stealthy, since users can ask ChatGPT to polish human writing. Because of these challenges, existing LLM detectors do not perform well, especially when detecting GPT-polished text (Sec. 2.2). Some experiences with identifying LLM-content have been reported in the literature, e.g., one study and another noted that ChatGPT output tends to be more objective, formal, focused, and fluent than human-content. But a holistic investigation of whether LLM-Content can be distinguished is still missing.

So in this paper we first identify three typical cases of using or abusing ChatGPT in academic writing: composing, completing, and polishing. We pick three representative disciplines: computer science for technical/engineering writing, physics for science writing, and humanities and social sciences for liberal arts writing. To cover a range of complex real-world scenarios, we used four different prompt patterns for each task in each discipline and collected a dataset, GPABench2, with 2.8 million human-written and ChatGPT-generated academic abstracts.

- User study + detectors
  - cohort of 155 evaluators (faculty, researchers, graduate students): recognition difficult by visual inspection, regardless of writing experience
  - second cohort of 87 with ground truth reference pairs: improved, still too low
  - 10+ SOTA online / open-source detectors, e.g. GPTZero: modest to poor; except LM-based (BERT, RoBERTa): better but excessive training effort
- CheckGPT
  - LM-based framework; feasibility of automated detection in a niche area
  - (1) black-box, deep learning, high accuracy vs human + SOTA detectors
  - (2) model-agnostic, plugin to pre-trained LMs (e.g. BERT) -> fewer trainable parameters
  - (3) generalized semantic patterns -> domain transfer with minimum fine-tuning
  - experiments: GPABench2; new domains, models, prompts; robustness to ChatGPT updates, human-modified GPT writing
- Contributions
  - GPABench2: cross-disciplinary corpus (human-written, GPT-written, GPT-completed, GPT-polished abstracts)
  - SOTA detectors evaluated; user study of 242 participants: humans can't distinguish regardless of experience, knowledge, reference
  - CheckGPT: deep-learning-based, model-agnostic; affordability, transferability, Robustness; (\sim 99% average accuracy)
- Ethics: Section 3 study approved (Human Research Protection Program, University of [Anonymized]); public abstracts; ChatGPT's API (with payment); dataset + tool open-sourced; community debate on AI writing tools; OpenAI education perspectives
- Organization: Sec 2 dataset + detectors; 3 user study; 4 CheckGPT; 5 experiments; 6 related work; 7 conclusion

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
ChatGPT, the Large Language Model (LLM) that debuted recently, has shown it can generate sophisticated texts with a human-like language style and quality. People are concerned that LLM-generated content (LLM-content) can be misused to abuse the trust systems we have, for example in cheating and plagiarism, or in phishing and romance scams. Many academic institutes and publishers have announced policies about using LLM content, but these policies are hard to enforce unless there is a tool that detects LLM content accurately.

Detecting LLM-content can be challenging because of the unique characters of LLM/ChatGPT: (1) the output of an LLM is a relevant, organized response with few grammar errors, like a human conversationalist would give; (2) because of the sampling mechanism of LLM output, the choice of words is stochastic, so the responses are distinct even when the same inquiry is repeated multiple times; and (3) misuse of LLM-content can be stealthy, since users can ask ChatGPT to polish human writing. Because of these challenges, existing LLM detectors do not perform well, especially when detecting GPT-polished text (Sec. 2.2). Some experiences with identifying LLM-content have been reported in the literature, e.g., one study and another noted that ChatGPT output tends to be more objective, formal, focused, and fluent than human-content. But a holistic investigation of whether LLM-Content can be distinguished is still missing.

So in this paper we first identify three typical cases of using or abusing ChatGPT in academic writing: composing, completing, and polishing. We pick three representative disciplines: computer science for technical/engineering writing, physics for science writing, and humanities and social sciences for liberal arts writing. To cover a range of complex real-world scenarios, we used four different prompt patterns for each task in each discipline and collected a dataset, GPABench2, with 2.8 million human-written and ChatGPT-generated academic abstracts.

Then we did an extensive field study with human evaluators to see if they can accurately distinguish LLM content when they are given a mixture of true and false samples. The first cohort had 155 evaluators, university faculty, researchers and graduate students, and it shows that recognizing LLM-content is difficult by visual inspection based on how the language appears, whether or not the person has experience writing research articles. A second cohort of 87 evaluators got ground truth data as references, which were pairs of human-written and GPT-generated abstracts. They were better at identifying human- and GPT-generated text, but the accuracy is still too low for reliable detection. We also test 10+ state-of-the-art online or open-source detectors on GPABench2, e.g., GPTZero, and they show modest to poor performance, except for the language-model-based detectors like BERT and RoBERTa, which get significantly better results but need excessive training efforts.

Last, we develop and evaluate a language-model-based detection framework called CheckGPT, to explore whether it is feasible to build automated tools for LLM-content detection in a niche area. CheckGPT has these advantages: (1) it is a black-box solution that uses deep learning frameworks to get high accuracy compared to humans and state-of-the-art (SOTA) LLM-content detectors. (2) CheckGPT uses a model-agnostic setting, so it can be used as a plugin to most pre-trained language models (e.g., BERT), and so the number of parameters that need training is reduced a lot. (3) Because it can learn generalized semantic patterns of LLM-content, CheckGPT has strong potential for domain transfer that only needs minimum fine-tuning efforts. Finally, we do comprehensive experiments to show CheckGPT's design goals and strengths: its performance on the GPABench2 dataset, how it transfers to new domains, new models and new prompts, and how robust it is against continuous updates of ChatGPT and against human-modified GPT writing.

Our main contributions are:

- • We present GPABench2, a cross-disciplinary corpus with human-written, GPT-written, GPT-completed, and GPT-polished research paper abstracts. GPABench2 could be a cornerstone for benchmarking GPT detectors and a valuable resource for designing new detection methods.

- • We evaluate the SOTA GPT detectors with GPABench2 and present how they perform. Also, with a user study of 242 participants, we show that human evaluators cannot distinguish between human-written and GPT-generated academic writing. This is the case regardless of experience, knowledge, and reference.

- • We present CheckGPT, a GPT-content detector that is deep-learning-based and model-agnostic, with validated benefits of affordability, transferability, and Robustness. We show the outstanding performance (\sim 99% average accuracy) of CheckGPT with extensive experiments.

Ethical Considerations. The user study in Section 3 was reviewed and approved by the Human Research Protection Program at the University of [Anonymized]. All the research paper abstracts we collected in Section 2 are open to the public. We used ChatGPT's API (with payment) to collect the GPT-generated abstracts. We have open-sourced the GPABench2 dataset and the CheckGPT tool. The academic community is actively discussing how AI writing assistance tools might create challenges for research and education. OpenAI has also posted its perspectives on the risks and opportunities related to education.

The rest of the paper is organized like this: Section 2 introduces the GPABench2 dataset and evaluates the open-source and commercial ChatGPT detectors, and Section 3 is a user study of ChatGPT-content detection. Section 4 has the technical details of CheckGPT and Section 5 the experimental results. Section 6 surveys the related literature and Section 7 concludes the paper.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The recently debuted Large Language Model (LLM) ChatGPT has shown an impressive ability to generate sophisticated texts with human-like language style and quality. Concerns have been raised that LLM-generated content (LLM-content) can be misused to abuse our trust systems, e.g., in cheating and plagiarism [1,2], or in phishing and romance scams [3,4]. While many academic institutes and publishers have announced policies on the usage of LLM content, such policies are hard to enforce unless we have a tool to accurately detect LLM content.

LLM-content detection can be challenging due to the unique characters of LLM/ChatGPT: (1) like a human conversationalist, LLM output is a relevant, organized response with a low level of grammar errors; (2) the sampling mechanism of LLM output makes the choice of words stochastic, so the responses are distinct even with multiple repeated inquiries; and (3) the misuse of LLM-content can be stealthy, since users can invoke ChatGPT to polish human writing. Facing these challenges, existing LLM detectors perform deficiently, especially in detecting GPT-polished text (Sec. 2.2). Some experiences in identifying LLM-content have been reported in the literature, e.g., [5] and [6] noted that ChatGPT output tends to be more objective, formal, focused, and fluent than human-content. However, a holistic investigation of the distinguishability of LLM-Content is still missing.

To this end, in this paper, we first identify three typical cases of using or abusing ChatGPT in academic writing: composing, completing, and polishing. We pick three representative disciplines for investigation: computer science for technical/engineering writing, physics for science writing, and humanities and social sciences for liberal arts writing. To address a range of complex real-world scenarios, we used four different prompt patterns for each task across each discipline and collected a dataset, GPABench2, with 2.8 million human-written and ChatGPT-generated academic abstracts.

Next, we conducted an extensive field study with human evaluators to assess whether they can accurately distinguish LLM content when provided with a mixture of true and false samples. The cohort of 155 evaluators, consisting of university faculty, researchers, and graduate students, shows that recognizing LLM-content by visual inspection of language appearance is difficult, with or without individual experience of writing research articles. A second cohort of 87 evaluators was provided with ground truth data as references: pairs of human-written and GPT-generated abstracts. While their capacity to identify human- and GPT-generated text improved, the accuracy is still too low for reliable detection. In addition, we test 10+ state-of-the-art online or open-source detectors on GPABench2, e.g., GPTZero, and show that they demonstrate modest to poor performance, except for language-model-based detectors like BERT and RoBERTa, which achieve significantly better results but require excessive training efforts.

Last, we develop and evaluate a language-model-based detection framework, named CheckGPT, to explore the feasibility of building automated tools for LLM-content detection in a niche area. CheckGPT has the following advantages: (1) it is a black-box solution that leverages deep learning frameworks to achieve high accuracy compared to human and state-of-the-art (SOTA) LLM-content detectors. (2) CheckGPT adopts a model-agnostic setting, so it can be treated as a plugin to most pre-trained language models (e.g., BERT); as a result, the number of parameters to be trained is largely reduced. (3) Due to its ability to learn generalized semantic patterns of LLM-content, CheckGPT shows strong potential for domain transfer that requires only minimum fine-tuning efforts. Finally, we conduct comprehensive experiments to demonstrate CheckGPT's design goals and strengths: its performance on the GPABench2 dataset, its transferability to new domains, new models, and new prompts, and its robustness against continuous updates of ChatGPT and against human-modified GPT writing.

In summary, our main contributions are:

- • We present GPABench2, a cross-disciplinary corpus consisting of human-written, GPT-written, GPT-completed, and GPT-polished research paper abstracts. GPABench2 can serve as a cornerstone for benchmarking GPT detectors and as a valuable resource to assist in the design of new detection methods.

- • We evaluate the SOTA GPT detectors with GPABench2 and present their performance. Meanwhile, with a user study of 242 participants, we show that human evaluators are unable to distinguish between human-written and GPT-generated academic writing, regardless of experience, knowledge, and reference.

- • We present CheckGPT, a deep-learning-based and model-agnostic GPT-content detector with validated benefits of affordability, transferability, and Robustness. We demonstrate the outstanding performance (\sim 99% average accuracy) of CheckGPT with extensive experiments.

Ethical Considerations. The user study in Section 3 was reviewed and approved by the Human Research Protection Program at the University of [Anonymized]. All the research paper abstracts collected in Section 2 are open to the public. We invoked ChatGPT's API (with payment) to collect the GPT-generated abstracts. The GPABench2 dataset and the CheckGPT tool have been open-sourced. The academic community is actively discussing how AI writing assistance tools may pose challenges to research and education [7,8,9]. OpenAI has also posted its perspectives on the education-related risks and opportunities [10].

The rest of the paper is organized as follows: We introduce the GPABench2 dataset and evaluate open-source and commercial ChatGPT detectors in Section 2, followed by a user study of ChatGPT-content detection in Section 3. We present the technical details of CheckGPT in Section 4 and the experimental results in Section 5. Finally, we survey related literature in Section 6 and conclude the paper in Section 7.
